ancestors.notes: Descent from Galician-Portuguese / medieval European Portuguese carried to Brazil from the 16th c.
Old Tupi (lingua geral) substrate: toponyms and everyday lexicon (abacaxi, mandioca, capim, jacare, peteca).
West-Central African (Kimbundu/Kikongo/Yoruba) adstrate from the enslaved population: samba, moleque, cacula, cafune, quilombo; often invoked for open pretonic vowels and syllable-timing tendencies.

vox_communis.measured: Board PER 0.3877 (n=33958) before PT_INITIAL_EX_VOICED, 0.3872 after it: 125 words start with ⟨ex⟩ plus a vowel, the gold writes [z] in all 125, and this spec now does too, one character each. The gold is epitran-derived and epitran's one Portuguese table (por-Latn) writes the European standard, which this spec does not (docs/languages/pt-BR.md counts the defining Brazilian features at 0 of 948 to 5 of 1637 in it). scripts/fold_pt_br_notation.py folds ten of its conventions out of BOTH sides cumulatively with the harness's own normalize() (broad) and levenshtein(): coda ʃ ʒ 0.3441, tʃi dʒi ~ ti di 0.3240, ɐ ~ a 0.2346, ɛ ~ e 0.1715, final o e ~ u i 0.1219, nasal vowel ~ vowel + n/m 0.0625, coda w ~ l 0.0550, ɲ ʎ ~ n l 0.0497, ʁ ~ ɾ 0.0429, ʷ dropped 0.0389; 26426 of 33958 words (77.8%) then match exactly. None of these is a contrast the spelling fails to write, so no valid_ceiling is recorded (T-2583). What the folds leave is the gold misreading the spelling, and it stays as scored: ⟨ss⟩ as two sibilants (981 of 995 ⟨ss⟩ words), intervocalic ⟨c⟩ before e/i and ⟨ç⟩ as z (privacidade, você), ⟨ch⟩ as k (achava), ⟨x⟩ after a diphthong as ks (baixo, deixar), ⟨ou⟩ as owu, and a final ⟨-am⟩ with no glide. This spec's readings of those letters stand (Barbosa & Albano 2004; Cunha & Cintra 1984). The ⟨ex-⟩ prefix inside a word (inexato, reexame) is [z] in the gold and [ʃ] here and stays a documented residue, since it needs a morphological cut. A coda ⟨x⟩ before a consonant (extra, texto) is ʃ here and s in the Brazilian standard, but this gold writes every coda sibilant ʃ, so it cannot measure that change and the change is not made.

allophone_rules.notes: Word-final ⟨-em / -ém / -êm⟩ is the nasal DIPHTHONG in Brazilian Portuguese too — bem [ˈbẽj̃], quem [ˈkẽj̃], também [tãˈbẽj̃], homem [ˈomẽj̃], ontem [ˈõtẽj̃] (Barbosa & Albano 2004: 230; Câmara Jr. 1970 and Mateus & d'Andrade 2000 not consulted). Unlike European Portuguese, BP does NOT centralise the nucleus to [ɐ̃]: it keeps the close-mid nasal [ẽ] and adds a nasal palatal offglide [j̃], so [̃]→[̃j̃] with the mid front nucleus left intact (hence no BR analogue of PT_FINAL_EM_NUCLEUS). Gated on the ORIGINAL preceding nucleus being a mid/high front vowel so ⟨-im -om -um⟩ (sim, bom, um) keep a plain nasal monophthong; word-final grapheme ⟨m⟩ only, so an ⟨em⟩ before a consonant (tempo, sempre) is excluded. Word-final ⟨-en⟩ of a learned noun takes the same diphthong: hífen [ˈifẽj̃], pólen, líquen, abdômen [abˈdomẽj̃]. Barbosa & Albano 2004 (JIPA 34(2): 230, speaker from the state of São Paulo): 'There are two post-stressed nasalised diphthongs: [ɐ̃w̃], as in bênção [ˈbẽsɐ̃w̃] ‘blessing’, and [ẽɪ̯̃], as in hífen [ˈifẽɪ̯̃] ‘hyphen’'; Ciberdúvidas answer 18963: 'No português do Brasil, em dialectos do português europeu e talvez nos países africanos onde se fala o português (não temos dados disponíveis), a grafia -em/-en(s) representa o ditongo [ẽj̃], distinguindo-se do ãe de mãe'; English Wikipedia 'Portuguese phonology' (Phonotactics, citing Mateus & d'Andrade 2000: 22, not opened): 'In Brazilian varieties, these words have a nasal diphthong ([abˈdõmẽj̃], spelled as abdômen)'. The nasalisation of the stressed [o] before the onset [m] in that last example is not modelled (see the ⟨ô⟩ finding in the pull request: the engine nasalises no stressed vowel before a nasal consonant).

Palatal offglide of word-final ⟨-ens⟩, the plural of the ⟨-em⟩ diphthong (see BR_FINAL_EM_GLIDE): the coda ⟨n⟩ before a word-final ⟨s⟩ after a mid front vowel is [̃j̃], so bens [ˈbẽj̃s], homens [ˈomẽj̃s], jovens [ˈʒovẽj̃s], viagens, parabéns. Ciberdúvidas answer 18963 lists the plural with the singular, with homem/homens and jovem/jovens as its examples: 'No português do Brasil, em dialectos do português europeu e talvez nos países africanos onde se fala o português (não temos dados disponíveis), a grafia -em/-en(s) representa o ditongo [ẽj̃], distinguindo-se do ãe de mãe'. Barbosa & Albano 2004 (JIPA 34(2): 230): 'Nasalised diphthongs are formed by combining [ẽ ɐ̃ õ ũ] with the offglide [j̃]'. English Wikipedia 'Portuguese phonology' (citing Cruz-Ferreira 1995, not opened): 'Nasal diphthongs occur mostly at the end of words (or followed by a final sibilant)'. Gated on the preceding mid front vowel, read before any other rule, so ⟨-ins -ons -uns⟩ keep a plain nasal monophthong (jardins, sons, atuns). Cristófaro Silva, Fonética e Fonologia do Português, was not available to read.

Word-final ⟨-am⟩ (3rd-person-plural verb ending) is the nasal diphthong [ɐ̃w̃] in Brazilian Portuguese — falam [ˈfalɐ̃w̃], custam [ˈkustɐ̃w̃], brilham [ˈbɾiʎɐ̃w̃] (Barbosa & Albano 2004: 230: 'With [ʊ̯̃], on the other hand, the only possibility is [ɐ̃ʊ̯̃]', and the passage writes discutiam [dʲiskutʃiɐ̃ʊ̯], p. 231; Câmara Jr. 1970 not consulted). The nucleus [ɐ̃] is supplied by the ⟨a⟩→[ɐ] nasal raise (PT_NASAL_A_RAISE) and this rule adds the [w̃] offglide to the coda ⟨m⟩ tilde: [̃]→[̃w̃]. Gated on the ORIGINAL preceding nucleus being low [a ɐ], disjoint from the ⟨-em⟩ glide; word-final ⟨am⟩ only occurs as this verb ending, and an ⟨am⟩ before a consonant (campo, ambos) is not word-final and keeps the plain nasal [ɐ̃].

Affrication of /t/ before a RAISED final unstressed vowel (leite [ˈlejt͡ʃi], gente [ˈʒẽt͡ʃi], sete [ˈsɛt͡ʃi]; Barbosa & Albano 2004: 228: 'Dental plosives are realised as affricates before [i] and [ɪ] in the variety illustrated here'; the passage writes norte [nɔɾtʃɪ], p. 231). The pre-lexical positional map affricates /t d/ only before a GRAPHEME ⟨i⟩ (before_i → tia [ˈt͡ʃiɐ]); it cannot reach the case where the trigger [i] is a word-final unstressed ⟨e⟩ that only becomes [i] post-lexically (positional selects the near-close [ɪ], raised to [i] by BR_RAISE_FINAL_E). This rule closes that feeding gap by conditioning on the FOLLOWING slot's underlying high front vowel — the near-close [ɪ] (the pre-raise realisation the rescorer reads on the neighbour) or a lexical [i] — so a ⟨t⟩ before it affricates regardless of whether the trigger was spelled ⟨i⟩ or a raised ⟨e⟩. It is a no-op where the positional map already produced [t͡ʃ] (the slot phoneme is no longer /t/). The non-palatalising nordeste (recife/norte/ce) and the conservative-dental caipira/sul/pt-UY varieties disable this rule by id.

Voiced counterpart of BR_AFFRIC_T_RAISED: /d/ affricates to [d͡ʒ] before a raised final unstressed vowel (tarde [ˈtaɾd͡ʒi], onde [ˈõd͡ʒi], pode [ˈpɔd͡ʒi]; Barbosa & Albano 2004: 228, the same statement as BR_AFFRIC_T_RAISED). Closes the same feeding gap where the trigger [i] is a word-final ⟨e⟩ raised only post-lexically (positional [ɪ] → [i] via BR_RAISE_FINAL_O/E), which the grapheme-⟨i⟩ positional before_i rule cannot see. No-op where the positional map already produced [d͡ʒ]. Disabled by id in the non-palatalising nordeste and conservative-dental caipira/sul/pt-UY varieties.

Coda-conditioned vowel nasalisation, general Portuguese, retained in Brazilian Portuguese (Barbosa & Albano 2004: 229: 'The archiphoneme /N/, in words such as canta /kaNta/ ‘(s/he) sings’ or irmã /iRˈmaN/ ‘sister’, triggers the nasalisation of a preceding vowel'; the nasalised [ɐ̃] is in the vowel table, santo [ˈsɐ̃ⁿtʊ]; Mateus & d'Andrade 2000 and Câmara Jr. 1970 not consulted): a vowel followed by a tautosyllabic (coda) nasal ⟨m/n⟩ nasalises and the nasal consonant is absorbed (campo, canto, ambos). The nasalisation is modelled pre-lexically by the positional 'm'/'n' before_consonant/word_final → [̃] (U+0303 combining tilde) map. This rule supplies only the VOWEL-QUALITY shift for ⟨a⟩: BP nasal /a/ is the raised central [ɐ̃] (campo [ˈkɐ̃pu]), so the oral [a] selected by the positional map raises to the ORAL base [ɐ] before the tilde — [ɐ]+[̃] = [ɐ̃]. The tilde comes only from the m/n slot, so no vowel is double-tilded. Fires only when the next slot is the tilde. A stressed vowel before an onset ⟨m n nh⟩ is nasalised by BR_NASAL_STRESSED_* (cama [ˈkɐ̃mɐ]); a pretonic one stays oral (camada [kaˈmadɐ]). The letter ⟨ã⟩ writes the same nasal vowel, so graphemes maps ⟨ã⟩ to [ɐ̃] (maçã [maˈsɐ̃], lã [ˈlɐ̃]). Barbosa & Albano (2004: 230) transcribe ímã as [ˈimɐ̃] 'magnet', and list the five nasalised vowels as [ĩ ẽ ɐ̃ õ ũ] (p. 229).

A word-initial pretonic ⟨en em⟩ is the raised nasal vowel [ĩ]: então [ĩˈtɐ̃w̃], embrulhava, envolto. Barbosa & Albano (2004: 231): 'Second, the sequence /eN/ is often pronounced as [ɪ̃], in pre-stressed, word-initial position, as in the words ɪ̃ˈtɐ̃ʊ̯ and ɪ̃ᵐbɾuʎavɐ (first and second passages).' The two transcribed passages on the same page have no word-initial pretonic [ẽ]: então is [ɪ̃] in both, and envolto is [ĩ] in both. This spec writes the close [ĩ], as BR_RAISE_FINAL_E writes the close [i] for the near-close [ɪ] of the same source. Carmo (2019, Estudos Linguísticos 48(2): 811) measures the raising of a word-initial pretonic /e/ before a coda nasal in north-western São Paulo state: Table 2 gives 'V/N/ 79,2% (773/976)', and the text says 'Cabe destacar, contudo, a frequência relativamente alta de aplicação do fenômeno nesse contexto: 79,2%'. Carmo writes the raised vowel [i]: '[i]n.tu.piu' (p. 811), '[i]ntortou' (p. 816). Carmo (2019: 803) quotes Battisti (1993: 95) for Rio Grande do Sul: 'a vogal e, em sílaba sem ataque, seguida de /S/ ou nasalizada (seguida de /N/), eleva-se quase que categoricamente'. Battisti (1993) was not opened. The raised vowel is the majority form, so it is the only output, and the [ẽ] of the other tokens is not in the lattice, as with BR_INFINITIVE_R_DROP. The rule takes an ⟨e⟩ that is the first grapheme of the word, in an unstressed syllable, before a coda nasal. An ⟨e⟩ after an onset keeps [ẽ] (temporal [tẽᵐpoˈɾaʊ̯], Barbosa & Albano 2004: 229), and so does a stressed one, whose nasal vowel is [ẽ] (sento [sẽⁿtʊ], p. 229). A nasal in the onset is not the archiphoneme /N/, so enorme and emoção keep an oral vowel, and Carmo (2019: 812) finds the raising blocked before a coda /R/ ('[e]r.guer', PR 0.007). The rule needs a consonant after the nasal, so the preposition em, a clitic with a word-final nasal, keeps the diphthong of BR_FINAL_EM_GLIDE. It stands before PT_NASAL_E_RAISE, so it also takes the open candidate of ⟨e⟩.

A word-initial pretonic ⟨e⟩ before a coda sibilant is [i]: estar [isˈta], esplendor [isplẽˈdoɾ], esmola [izˈmolɐ]. Carmo (2019, Estudos Linguísticos 48(2): 811) measures the raising of a word-initial pretonic /e/ in north-western São Paulo state. Table 2 gives 'V/S/ 99,5% (1449/1457)' with relative weight 0.881, and the text says 'o contexto de pretônica seguida por consoante sibilante em coda, como em [i]s.co.la e [i]s.fa.re.la, favorece a aplicação do processo, com PR 0.881'. Barbosa & Albano (2004: 231) transcribe todo o esplendor as 'todʊɪspleⁿˈdoɾ', with the raised vowel. This spec writes the close [i], as BR_INITIAL_EN_RAISE does for the same source. The rule takes an ⟨e⟩ that is the first grapheme of the word, in an unstressed syllable, before a sibilant that a consonant follows, so the sibilant is a coda. A sibilant in the onset keeps the vowel (essencial, Esaú), and so does a stressed ⟨e⟩ (este, esse). The sibilant list holds the palatal [ʃ ʒ] for the regional specs that write the coda that way. The sibilant must be the letter ⟨s⟩. A pretonic ⟨ex⟩ before a consonant (explicar, extrair) has the same coda /S/, but no opened source states its raising. Carmo (2019: 807, 815) names the prefixes 'ex-/es-' and gives only ⟨es⟩ examples ('[i]sclareci', '[i]spalma'), so the ⟨ex⟩ words keep [e] until a source counts them.

Vowel-quality companion of the coda-nasalisation (see PT_NASAL_A_RAISE; Mateus & d'Andrade 2000: ch.2). BP nasal /e/ is the close-mid [ẽ], so the open [ɛ] raises to the oral base [e] before the nasalisation tilde — [e]+[̃] = [ẽ] (tempo [ˈtẽpu], sempre). Surface is oral [e]; the tilde is supplied only by the coda m/n slot (no double tilde). Fires only before the tilde, so this rule leaves an ⟨e⟩ before an onset ⟨m n⟩ alone; BR_NASAL_STRESSED_E nasalises the stressed one (pena [ˈpẽnɐ]).

Vowel-quality companion of the coda-nasalisation (see PT_NASAL_A_RAISE; Mateus & d'Andrade 2000: ch.2). BP nasal /o/ is the close-mid [õ], so the open [ɔ] raises to the oral base [o] before the nasalisation tilde — [o]+[̃] = [õ] (bom [ˈbõ], onde). Surface is oral [o]; the tilde is supplied only by the coda m/n slot (no double tilde). Fires only before the tilde, so this rule leaves an ⟨o⟩ before an onset ⟨m n⟩ alone; BR_NASAL_STRESSED_O nasalises the stressed one (fome [ˈfõmi]). High vowels ⟨i u⟩ need no companion rule — [ĩ ũ] share the oral base [i u] (sim [ˈsĩ], mundo [ˈmũdu]).

Phonetic nasalisation of a stressed vowel before a nasal consonant in the next onset: cama [ˈkɐ̃mɐ], ano [ˈɐ̃nu], tema [ˈtẽmɐ], soma [ˈsõmɐ], cima [ˈsĩmɐ], ganho [ˈɡɐ̃ɲu]. Barbosa & Albano (2004: 229): 'There is a phonetic contrast of five nasalised allophones in stressed position before the archiphoneme /N/ (which induces the so-called phonological nasalisation, illustrated by the preceding list), as well as before heterosyllabic nasal consonants (which triggers the so-called phonetic nasalisation): [ĩ ẽ ɐ̃ õ ũ]. The latter condition is exemplified by the following list: (em) cima sĩmɐ ‘above’, sema sẽmɐ ‘seme’, sama sɐ̃mɐ ‘pine tree leaf’, soma sõmɐ ‘sum’, (em) suma sũmɐ ‘to sum up’.' The consonant table gives ganho [ˈɡɐ̃ɲʊ] (p. 228), and the transcribed passage writes numa [ˈnũma] (p. 231). Only five nasal vowels exist, so an open [ɛ ɔ] surfaces as the close-mid [ẽ õ]. Mendonça & Oliveira (2019: 45) state the same context as categorical: 'vogais acentuadas seguidas de uma consoante nasal sempre serão nasalizadas, como em [ˈkãmɐ] “cama”, e vogais seguidas da nasal palatal terão nasalização categórica, como em [ˈbãɲʊ] “banho” e [kõˈɲesʊ] “conheço”'. Moraes & Wetzels (1992: 155), citing Abaurre (1973), report the opposite for São Paulo: 'em São Paulo, com freqüência, não se nasalizam as vogais tônicas: fôme, hòmem, telefòne, Antònio', with cama ['kɐma]. This rule follows the two sources that describe the nasalised form as the norm; the oral São Paulo form is a documented variant. The rule reads the next slot's phoneme, so a coda ⟨m n⟩ (written as the nasal tilde by the positional map) is left to PT_NASAL_*_RAISE, and a pretonic vowel before an onset ⟨m n⟩ stays oral (banana [baˈnɐ̃nɐ], camada [kaˈmadɐ]).

Barbosa & Albano (2004: 229): 'In pre-stressed position, there is a ten-vowel phonetic contrast, where the quality of the corresponding stressed vowel is roughly preserved: [i e a o u ĩ ẽ ɐ̃ õ ũ]. Mendonça & Oliveira (2019: 45) state the same context as categorical: 'vogais acentuadas seguidas de uma consoante nasal sempre serão nasalizadas, como em [ˈkãmɐ] “cama”, e vogais seguidas da nasal palatal terão nasalização categórica, como em [ˈbãɲʊ] “banho” e [kõˈɲesʊ] “conheço”'. Only an unstressed vowel before /m n/ varies. Moraes & Wetzels (1992: 155), citing Abaurre (1973), report the opposite for São Paulo: 'em São Paulo, com freqüência, não se nasalizam as vogais tônicas: fôme, hòmem, telefòne, Antònio', with cama ['kɐma]. This rule follows the two sources that describe the nasalised form as the norm; the oral São Paulo form is a documented variant. The rule reads the next slot's phoneme, so a coda ⟨m n⟩ (written as the nasal tilde by the positional map) is left to PT_NASAL_*_RAISE, and a pretonic vowel before an onset ⟨m n⟩ stays oral (banana [baˈnɐ̃nɐ], camada [kaˈmadɐ]).

Pretonic nasalisation before the palatal nasal: ganhar [ɡɐ̃ˈɲaɾ], senhor [sẽˈɲoɾ]. Barbosa & Albano (2004: 229): 'In pre-stressed position, there is a ten-vowel phonetic contrast, where the quality of the corresponding stressed vowel is roughly preserved: [i e a o u ĩ ẽ ɐ̃ õ ũ]. Nasalised vowels in this position surface either before /N/ (e.g. temporal tẽᵐpoˈɾaʊ̯ ‘temporal’) or before /ɲ/ (e.g. ganhar gɐ̃ˈɲaɾ ‘(to) win’).' A pretonic vowel before /m n/ is not in that list and stays oral.

Phonetic nasalisation of a stressed vowel before a nasal consonant in the next onset: cama [ˈkɐ̃mɐ], ano [ˈɐ̃nu], tema [ˈtẽmɐ], soma [ˈsõmɐ], cima [ˈsĩmɐ], ganho [ˈɡɐ̃ɲu]. Barbosa & Albano (2004: 229): 'There is a phonetic contrast of five nasalised allophones in stressed position before the archiphoneme /N/ (which induces the so-called phonological nasalisation, illustrated by the preceding list), as well as before heterosyllabic nasal consonants (which triggers the so-called phonetic nasalisation): [ĩ ẽ ɐ̃ õ ũ]. The latter condition is exemplified by the following list: (em) cima sĩmɐ ‘above’, sema sẽmɐ ‘seme’, sama sɐ̃mɐ ‘pine tree leaf’, soma sõmɐ ‘sum’, (em) suma sũmɐ ‘to sum up’.' The consonant table gives ganho [ˈɡɐ̃ɲʊ] (p. 228), and the transcribed passage writes numa [ˈnũma] (p. 231). Only five nasal vowels exist, so an open [ɛ ɔ] surfaces as the close-mid [ẽ õ]. Mendonça & Oliveira (2019: 45) state the same context as categorical: 'vogais acentuadas seguidas de uma consoante nasal sempre serão nasalizadas, como em [ˈkãmɐ] “cama”, e vogais seguidas da nasal palatal terão nasalização categórica, como em [ˈbãɲʊ] “banho” e [kõˈɲesʊ] “conheço”'. Only an unstressed vowel before /m n/ varies. Moraes & Wetzels (1992: 155), citing Abaurre (1973), report the opposite for São Paulo: 'em São Paulo, com freqüência, não se nasalizam as vogais tônicas: fôme, hòmem, telefòne, Antònio', with cama ['kɐma]. This rule follows the two sources that describe the nasalised form as the norm; the oral São Paulo form is a documented variant. The rule reads the next slot's phoneme, so a coda ⟨m n⟩ (written as the nasal tilde by the positional map) is left to PT_NASAL_*_RAISE, and a pretonic vowel before an onset ⟨m n⟩ stays oral (banana [baˈnɐ̃nɐ], camada [kaˈmadɐ]).

Pretonic nasalisation before the palatal nasal: ganhar [ɡɐ̃ˈɲaɾ], senhor [sẽˈɲoɾ]. Barbosa & Albano (2004: 229): 'In pre-stressed position, there is a ten-vowel phonetic contrast, where the quality of the corresponding stressed vowel is roughly preserved: [i e a o u ĩ ẽ ɐ̃ õ ũ]. Nasalised vowels in this position surface either before /N/ (e.g. temporal tẽᵐpoˈɾaʊ̯ ‘temporal’) or before /ɲ/ (e.g. ganhar gɐ̃ˈɲaɾ ‘(to) win’).' A pretonic vowel before /m n/ is not in that list and stays oral.

A coda /S/ takes the voicing of a following voiced consonant: mesmo [ˈmezmu], desde [ˈdezd͡ʒi], Lisboa [lizˈboɐ]. Barbosa & Albano (2004: 229): 'The archiphoneme /S/ surfaces either as a voiced or as a voiceless alveolar fricative. As in most varieties, it tends to assimilate the voicing of the following sound.' The rule reads the next slot's phoneme inside the word. Across a word boundary the same assimilation is the sandhi rule BR_FINAL_S_VOICING.

The voicing assimilation of BR_CODA_S_VOICED for a lect whose positional map writes the coda sibilant as the palatal [ʃ] (mesmo [ˈmeʒmu]). Same source: Barbosa & Albano (2004: 229), 'it tends to assimilate the voicing of the following sound'. In this spec no coda ⟨s z⟩ reaches [ʃ], so the rule fires only in the regional specs that inherit it.

An ⟨r⟩ at the start of a syllable after a coda consonant is the strong rhotic, not the tap: honra [ˈõʁɐ], genro [ˈʒẽʁu], Israel [izʁaˈɛw], desrespeito. Cristófaro Silva (2025: 240): 'Nos demais contextos, o R-forte ocorre sempre em início de sílaba que pode ser: início de sílaba que coincide com início de palavra (rapaz, rio, rosa etc.); início de sílaba em meio de palavra (carro, terra) ou início de sílaba após consoante (Israel, desrespeito etc.).' Cristófaro Silva (2025: 243) names the three consonants: 'uma sibilante (Israel), uma nasal fonológica sem manifestação fonética (honra) ou uma lateral que pode ou não ser vocalizada (guelra)', and reports a tap after the vocalised lateral as an innovation ([ˈgɛʊhɐ] ~ [ˈgɛʊɾɐ]). The rule reads the previous slot's phoneme: the nasal tilde of a coda ⟨m n⟩ or a coda sibilant. The tap of an onset cluster (prato, abraço) and the tap after a diphthong (feira, Europa) are untouched. After a vocalised ⟨l⟩ the spec keeps the tap, the variant Cristófaro Silva reports (guelra, melro). A regional spec with another strong rhotic overrides this rule by id.

A word-final ⟨r⟩ keeps the tap when the word is not an infinitive or a future subjunctive: mar [ˈmaɾ], lugar [luˈɡaɾ], mulher [muˈʎeɾ], qualquer [kwawˈkeɾ], militar [miliˈtaɾ]. Barbosa & Albano (2004: 228) state the drop for infinitives only. Callou, Moraes & Leite (1998: 66): 'Nos não-verbos, em que o R não carreia informação morfológica, o peso relativo é baixo'; p. 67, for nouns 'a perda do R sendo praticamente bloqueada em vocábulos monossilábicos'. The rule rewrites the tap to itself and stands before BR_INFINITIVE_R_DROP, so the first rule that matches is this one. The list holds every word that ends in an unaccented ⟨-ar -er -ir⟩ and that the English Wiktionary (kaikki.org Portuguese extract) gives with no infinitive or future-subjunctive reading (lugar, mulher, quer), and the noun-verb homographs whose non-verb tokens outnumber the verb tokens in the UD Portuguese treebanks Bosque, CINTIL, DANTEStocks, GSD and PetroGold (poder 133 against 61, olhar 33 against 15, andar 24 against 21); a name or a foreign token does not count against a verb reading. A word that Wiktionary does not hold is listed when its treebank tokens are mostly not verbs (Itamar, Neymar). A child spec whose own rule rewrites the final tap switches this rule and the two drop rules off by id.

The word-final tap of an infinitive drops: falar [faˈla], comer [koˈme], partir [paɾˈt͡ʃi], fazer [faˈze]. Barbosa & Albano (2004: 228-229): 'The tap is the preferred realisation for /R/ in the variety presented here. In infinitives, however, this sound usually drops word-finally except if followed by a vowel.' Callou, Moraes & Leite (1998: 66) give the cue that the spelling carries: 'A perda do R é mais freqüente nos verbos: o infinitivo e a primeira e terceira pessoas do futuro do subjuntivo são marcados em português tanto pela presença do R final quanto pela tonicidade da sílaba que contém o segmento (comer versus come)'. Cristófaro Silva (2025: 242): 'O cancelamento do R-pósvocálico ocorre em maiores índices em formas verbais de infinitivo, mas também ocorre, em menores índices, em formas nominais'. The rule takes a word-final ⟨r⟩ after an unaccented ⟨a e i⟩ in the stressed syllable, so a word with a written accent on an earlier syllable keeps the tap (açúcar, revólver). The future subjunctive has the same ending and drops with it (fizer [fiˈze]). The non-verbs of the same shape are in BR_FINAL_R_NONVERB, which stands before this rule. The infinitive ⟨-or⟩ of pôr and its compounds is BR_INFINITIVE_R_DROP_POR. The drop is a rate, not a categorical rule: verbs 73-82 % in Rio de Janeiro (Callou, Moraes & Leite 1998: 67), 83-98 % in the Northeast capitals (Callou, Serra & Cunha 2015: 207), and 93 % among young women in Porto Alegre (Callou, Serra & Cunha 2015: 202). A pause after the verb lowers the rate, and the drop stays the majority: Aracaju verbs before a pause 88 of 129, 68 % (Callou, Serra & Cunha 2015: 205). Careful speech keeps the tap: Barbosa & Albano print it in their citation forms (pagar [paˈɡaɾ], p. 227; acabar [akaˈbaɾ], p. 228; ganhar [ɡɐ̃ˈɲaɾ], p. 229) and in the read passage (soprar com, p. 231). Before a vowel of the next word the tap stays (Barbosa & Albano 2004: 229); this rule reads one word and does not see the next one.

The drop of BR_INFINITIVE_R_DROP for the infinitive ⟨-or⟩: pôr [ˈpo], compor [kõˈpo], propor [pɾoˈpo], and for the future subjunctive for [ˈfo] (se eu for). Same sources. A final ⟨-or⟩ is otherwise a noun or an adjective (amor, maior, vapor), so the rule names the words. The list holds the ⟨-or -ôr⟩ words that the English Wiktionary (kaikki.org Portuguese extract) gives as an infinitive or a future subjunctive.

Blocks BR_EPENTHESIS between the two halves of a doubled consonant letter, which only loans spell: buffer [bufˈfeɾ], buffet, Zotti, Uppsala. The rule rewrites the first half to itself, and it stands before BR_EPENTHESIS, so the first rule that matches is this one. It names the second half in followed_by_phoneme, so the engine's geminate protection lets it act on the first half. Curioletti & Sandri (2019, Cadernos do IL 59, PDF p. 6): 'Daí decorre a epêntese, que só se aplica em sequências não-homorgânicas, como em capto [kapitu], e não em geminadas subjacentes (carro) ou de superfície (carta) (MONARETTO, 1997, p. 188)'. Monaretto (1997) was not opened. A doubled ⟨t d⟩ is gated before any vowel, because [t t͡ʃ] and [d d͡ʒ] are homorganic. A doubled ⟨c g⟩ is gated only where both letters spell the same stop: ⟨cc⟩ before ⟨e i⟩ is [ks] (occipital) and ⟨gg⟩ before ⟨e i⟩ is [ɡʒ], two non-homorganic obstruents, which the rule still breaks.

Blocks the BR_EPENTHESIS rules inside the loan spelling ⟨tch⟩, which writes the affricate [tʃ] before any vowel: tchau [ˈtʃaw], tchê, tcheco. The rule rewrites the [t] to itself, and it stands before BR_EPENTHESIS, as the BR_GEMINATE rules do. pt.wiktionary gives tchau as '{{AFI|/tʃaʊ/|pt}}', one syllable with no vowel between [t] and [ʃ]. Barbosa & Albano (2004: 228) list [t͡ʃ] in the row 'Affricates' of their consonant chart. ⟨tch⟩ writes that one segment, not a two-obstruent sequence. The spec writes it as [t] and [ʃ] in a row, because ⟨t⟩ and ⟨ch⟩ are two graphemes. The phoneme list holds [t͡ʃ] for pt-BR-x-cuiaba, which reads ⟨ch⟩ as [t͡ʃ].

Vowel epenthesis between two obstruents: advogado [ad͡ʒivoˈɡadu], absurdo [abiˈsuɾdu], opção [opiˈsɐ̃w̃], obter [obiˈteɾ], psicologia [pisikoloˈʒiɐ]. Barbosa & Albano (2004: 227): 'By contrast, BP exhibits vowel epenthesis, breaking most two-obstruent sequences. For phonotactic reasons common to both BP and EP, one of the consonants is always an apical: psicologia pisɪkoloʒiɐ or pɪsikoloʒiɐ ‘psychology’ in BP vs. psɪkoloʒiɐ in EP. The epenthetic vowel is always [i] or [ɪ]'. The inserted vowel is [i], so a preceding /t d/ affricates on the second allophone pass (advogado). Scope: a stop or labiodental fricative before an obstruent. A coda sibilant is an archiphoneme /S/ and is not a target (festa). A nasal or liquid after the stop is not an obstruent, so ritmo and pneu are outside the source's statement and stay as spelled. The rule is held to an unstressed syllable that has a nucleus after it. A stop after the stressed vowel is BR_EPENTHESIS_POSTTONIC. The process varies with position and context. Collischonn (2004: 66-67), on southern Brazilian speech, measures epenthesis in 69% of pretonic and 24% of post-tonic tokens, and by following consonant 89% before a non-sibilant fricative (advogado), 77% before a nasal (mogno), 44% before a stop (rapto) and 34% before a sibilant (opção). The base follows the São Paulo description of Barbosa & Albano.

Vowel epenthesis after the stressed vowel: capto [ˈkapitu], pacto [ˈpakitu], rapto [ˈʁapitu]. It is BR_EPENTHESIS for a stop or a labiodental fricative after the stressed vowel, before an obstruent, with a nucleus after it. A word-final cluster (chips, blitz) has no nucleus after it and stays as spelled. A cluster at the start of the stressed syllable (pseudo, psique) has no vowel before it, so it is outside this rule and stays as spelled. Curioletti & Sandri (2019, Cadernos do IL 59, PDF p. 6): 'Daí decorre a epêntese, que só se aplica em sequências não-homorgânicas, como em capto [kapitu], e não em geminadas subjacentes (carro) ou de superfície (carta) (MONARETTO, 1997, p. 188)'. Monaretto (1997) was not opened. Collischonn (2004: 66) reports Câmara Jr.: 'Como observa Câmara Jr. (1969, p. 28), na posição postônica a vogal se reduz, da mesma forma que ocorre com a vogal da penúltima sílaba de proparoxítonas, sendo, portanto, idênticas as pautas prosódicas de rapto e rápido.' Câmara Jr. was not opened. Barbosa & Albano (2004: 227) state the epenthesis for 'most two-obstruent sequences' and do not restrict it by position. The rate after the stress is lower than before it. Collischonn (2004: 67, Tabela 1) counts 49 of 206 post-tonic tokens (24 %) against 225 of 325 pretonic tokens (69 %) in the speech of Porto Alegre, Florianópolis and Curitiba, and reads the post-tonic grammar without epenthesis as the preferred one (p. 76: 'na pauta postônica: ALINH-PÉ-DIR >> CODA-COND NÃO HÁ EPÊNTESE Ordenação preferida'). Silveira & Seara (2009, Revista do GEL 6(2): 22, Tabela 6) count 77 of 100 post-tonic tokens for the two women and 49 of 100 for the two men of a Florianópolis reading task. No source measures the rate in São Paulo, so the base follows the statement of Barbosa & Albano and the forms of Curioletti & Sandri and Câmara Jr. pt-BR-x-sul, pt-BR-x-floripa and pt-BR-x-pr switch the rule off by id on Collischonn's count. The stress count folds a syllable whose only vowel a rule inserted into the syllable before it, so the mark stays on the stressed syllable.

Vowel epenthesis in a two-obstruent cluster that opens a stressed word-initial syllable: pseudo [piˈsewdu], psique [piˈsiki]. It is BR_EPENTHESIS for the first consonant of the word when that consonant stands in the stressed syllable. Barbosa & Albano (2004: 227): 'BP exhibits vowel epenthesis, breaking most two-obstruent sequences. For phonotactic reasons common to both BP and EP, one of the consonants is always an apical: psicologia pisɪkoloʒiɐ or pɪsikoloʒiɐ ‘psychology’ in BP vs. psɪkoloʒiɐ in EP. The epenthetic vowel is always [i] or [ɪ]'. The statement does not restrict the process by stress, and its example breaks a word-initial cluster. Nascimento (2015, Epêntese vocálica em encontros consonantais por falantes brasileiros de inglês como língua estrangeira, master's thesis, UNESP Araraquara, pp. 62-63) reports the analysis of Collischonn (1996: 151-155): a word-initial consonant that the syllable cannot hold takes the vowel to its right, with the forms 'pneu [pi'new], Ptolomeu [pitolo'mew]'. The vowel of pneu stands before a stressed nucleus. Collischonn (1996) was not opened. Romano & Seabra (2017, Signum 20(1), pp. 284-285) find the vowel in every ALiB response to aftosa, pneu and advogado from 220 speakers of Paraná and São Paulo: 'houve a ocorrência da vogal epentética em todos os inquéritos, seja com a realização da vogal alta anterior [i] ou da vogal média anterior [e], tratando-se, portanto, de uma regra categórica no corpus analisado'. pneu has a nasal after the stop, so it is outside this rule, which keeps the obstruent scope of BR_EPENTHESIS. Collischonn (2004: 65) codes the position of the lost consonant as a factor ('inicial (psicólogo) ou medial (opção)') and gives no rate for the word-initial position, so the regional specs inherit the rule. A cluster inside the word is split by the syllabifier and reads BR_EPENTHESIS or BR_EPENTHESIS_POSTTONIC. The stress count keeps the mark after the inserted vowel, before the stressed nucleus.

Final unstressed vowel raising in the ⟨-es⟩ ending (see the source note below): an unstressed word-final ⟨e⟩ raises to close [i] before the plural/2sg coda ⟨-s⟩ exactly as it does word-finally without the ⟨s⟩ (dente [ˈdẽt͡ʃi] : dentes [ˈdẽt͡ʃis]; pote : potes; estes [ˈest͡ʃis]; pires [ˈpiɾis]). The bare-final case is BR_RAISE_FINAL_E; here the ⟨s⟩ intervenes so the nucleus is not word-final and the pre-lexical map leaves it [e] (posttonic nucleus_unstressed), which this rule raises. Gated `unstressed` so a stressed ⟨-ês/-és⟩ monosyllable keeps its mid vowel (três [ˈtɾes], mês [ˈmes], dez [ˈdɛs] — the last is [ɛ] and untargeted anyway). `followed_by_2 = word_boundary` restricts it to the true ending, so a medial ⟨e⟩ before a tautosyllabic ⟨s⟩+C (vespa, festa) is untouched. Feeds the /t d/ affrication (BR_AFFRIC_*_RAISED) on the preceding slot, which is why the pt-BR spec runs the allophone pass twice (allophone_passes): the affrication reads this rule's raised [i] only on the second pass. Barbosa & Albano (2004) write the post-stressed vowels as the non-peripheral [ɪ ɐ ʊ]: 'In post-stressed position, the variety studied here contrasts four oral vowels' (p. 229), saque [ˈsakɪ], saco [ˈsakʊ], and 'In post-stressed position, vowels are realised as non-peripherical allophones' (p. 230). This spec writes the close [i u], the broad value to which final /e o/ neutralise, and keeps the near-close [ɪ ʊ] as the pre-lexical value. The choice is a notation convention, not a different pronunciation. Câmara Jr. (1970) is cited for the neutralisation; the edition was not consulted.

Voiced-vowel counterpart of BR_RAISE_FINAL_ES: an unstressed word-final ⟨o⟩ raises to close [u] before the plural coda ⟨-s⟩ (gato [ˈɡatu] : gatos [ˈɡatus]; tios [ˈt͡ʃius]; montes/pontos). The bare-final case is BR_RAISE_FINAL_O; here the ⟨s⟩ intervenes so the pre-lexical map leaves the nucleus [o] (posttonic), which this rule raises. Gated `unstressed` so a stressed ⟨-ós/-ôs⟩ (nós [ˈnɔs], avós, pôs) keeps its mid vowel; `followed_by_2 = word_boundary` restricts it to the ending so a medial ⟨o⟩ before ⟨s⟩+C (mosca, gosto) is untouched. Barbosa & Albano (2004) write the post-stressed vowels as the non-peripheral [ɪ ɐ ʊ]: 'In post-stressed position, the variety studied here contrasts four oral vowels' (p. 229), saque [ˈsakɪ], saco [ˈsakʊ], and 'In post-stressed position, vowels are realised as non-peripherical allophones' (p. 230). This spec writes the close [i u], the broad value to which final /e o/ neutralise, and keeps the near-close [ɪ ʊ] as the pre-lexical value. The choice is a notation convention, not a different pronunciation. Câmara Jr. (1970) is cited for the neutralisation; the edition was not consulted.

Post-stressed final /a/ before the plural or verbal ⟨-s⟩ is [ɐ], as it is word-finally without the ⟨s⟩ (casa [ˈkazɐ] : casas [ˈkazɐs]; festas, falas). Barbosa & Albano (2004: 229-230): 'In post-stressed position, the variety studied here contrasts four oral vowels, including a centralised version of [e] (in this variety, only in non-final post-stressed position under antepenultimate stress, as in ópera [ˈɔpe̞ɾɐ] ‘opera’ and número [ˈnũme̞ɾʊ] ‘number’): [ɪ ɐ ʊ e̞]'; [a] is not one of them. The ⟨s⟩ closes the syllable, so the pre-lexical posttonic map leaves the nucleus [a], and this rule reduces it. The rule takes the position the source states: `posttonic` keeps a stressed ⟨-ás⟩ (gás, atrás) at [a], and `requires_other_nucleus` keeps a monosyllable out, so the clitics as and às, which have no stress of their own and so no post-stressed syllable, are not reduced by this rule. `followed_by_2 = word_boundary` keeps a medial ⟨a⟩ before ⟨s⟩+C (pasta) untouched. [ʃ] is listed for the children whose coda /S/ is palatal.

Final unstressed vowel raising (see the source note below): word-final unstressed /e/ raises to close [i] (leite → [ˈlejt͡ʃi], dente → [ˈdẽt͡ʃi]). The pre-lexical map selects the near-close [ɪ] word-finally; this pass writes the close [i]. Targeting only the reduced [ɪ] (not underlying /e/) leaves conservative dialects that retain a final [e] untouched, so the delta stays inheritable. Barbosa & Albano (2004) write the post-stressed vowels as the non-peripheral [ɪ ɐ ʊ]: 'In post-stressed position, the variety studied here contrasts four oral vowels' (p. 229), saque [ˈsakɪ], saco [ˈsakʊ], and 'In post-stressed position, vowels are realised as non-peripherical allophones' (p. 230). This spec writes the close [i u], the broad value to which final /e o/ neutralise, and keeps the near-close [ɪ ʊ] as the pre-lexical value. The choice is a notation convention, not a different pronunciation. Câmara Jr. (1970) is cited for the neutralisation; the edition was not consulted.

Final unstressed vowel raising (see the source note below): word-final unstressed /o/ raises to close [u] (gato → [ˈɡatu]). Pretonic reduction is markedly weaker in BP than EP and is not modelled: BP keeps distinct pretonic /e o/, so only the final position raises. Targets the reduced [ʊ] only, leaving conservative dialects that retain a final [o] untouched. Barbosa & Albano (2004) write the post-stressed vowels as the non-peripheral [ɪ ɐ ʊ]: 'In post-stressed position, the variety studied here contrasts four oral vowels' (p. 229), saque [ˈsakɪ], saco [ˈsakʊ], and 'In post-stressed position, vowels are realised as non-peripherical allophones' (p. 230). This spec writes the close [i u], the broad value to which final /e o/ neutralise, and keeps the near-close [ɪ ʊ] as the pre-lexical value. The choice is a notation convention, not a different pronunciation. Câmara Jr. (1970) is cited for the neutralisation; the edition was not consulted.

Lexically CLOSE stressed ⟨o⟩ = [o] for this curated set of frequent lexemes, overriding the pre-lexical default (which is the open [ɔ] in the European standard and, by inheritance, ambiguous elsewhere). Portuguese stressed mid-vowel height is lexically/etymologically fixed and not predictable from spelling — ⟨sopa⟩ [ˈsopɐ] (close, < Gmc *suppa) vs ⟨sova⟩ [ˈsɔvɐ] (open) are spelled and stressed alike (Mateus & d'Andrade 2000: ch.3 'The vowels'; Vigário 2003). This rule pins ONLY the stressed-vowel height and lets reduction, rhotics, sandhi and affrication run normally, so it inherits cleanly to every pt-PT / pt-BR dialect child. Includes the ⟨-oso⟩ masculine adjectival suffix (saboroso, gostoso, famoso), which is regularly close [o] against its open [ɔ] feminine ⟨-osa⟩ (PT_LEX_OPEN_O). SEED LIST — the arbitration-confirmed frequent lexemes; the long tail of Portuguese mid-vowel lexemes is documented residual, to be extended from Mateus & d'Andrade / a pronouncing dictionary.

Lexically CLOSE stressed ⟨e⟩ = [e] for this curated set, overriding the pre-lexical default (open [ɛ] first in the European standard). Stressed mid-vowel height is a lexical fact in Portuguese (⟨fresco⟩ [ˈfɾe(ʃ)ku] close vs many open ⟨e⟩ lexemes spelled alike; Mateus & d'Andrade 2000: ch.3; Vigário 2003). Pins only the vowel height, inherits cleanly. SEED LIST — documented residual for the tail.

Lexically OPEN stressed ⟨o⟩ = [ɔ] for this curated set, overriding the pre-lexical default (which is the close [o] first selected in Brazilian and non-reducing inheritors, giving the wrong height for these lexemes). Height is a lexical/morphological fact (Mateus & d'Andrade 2000: ch.3; Vigário 2003): the 3sg present of ⟨-ar/-er⟩ verbs opens the stressed root vowel (mora, corre, espera), and the ⟨-osa⟩ feminine adjectival suffix is open [ɔ] (famosa, gostosa) against its close [o] masculine ⟨-oso⟩ (PT_LEX_CLOSE_O). This rule pins ONLY the stressed-vowel height (reduction, rhotics, l-vocalisation, affrication run normally), so it inherits cleanly to every pt-PT / pt-BR dialect child. SEED LIST — arbitration-confirmed lexemes; the tail is documented residual.

Lexically OPEN stressed ⟨e⟩ = [ɛ] for this curated set, overriding the pre-lexical default where a close [e] is selected (Brazilian and non-reducing inheritors). Includes items whose open height is etymological (Latin short ĕ: terra, serra), morphological (3sg present espera; the copula era) or simply lexical (dez). Mateus & d'Andrade 2000: ch.3; Vigário 2003. Pins only the vowel height and inherits cleanly. SEED LIST — documented residual for the tail.

The ⟨x⟩ of the trazer preterite/subjunctive stem ⟨troux-⟩ is [s], not the default [ʃ] (trouxe [ˈtɾo(w)sɨ] / BP [ˈtɾosi]; Cunha & Cintra 1984, §on ⟨x⟩; the value of orthographic ⟨x⟩ is lexically unpredictable — [ʃ] peixe, [s] trouxe/próximo, [ks] fixo, [z] exame). Keyed on the lexeme because no phonological context separates the trouxe ⟨x⟩=[s] from the luxo ⟨x⟩=[ʃ]; gated on grapheme ⟨x⟩ so it never touches a ⟨ch⟩ or lexical [ʃ]. Pins only the consonant, so vowel reduction and the surrounding processes run normally and it inherits to every pt child. SEED — the broader ⟨x⟩=[s]/[ks]/[z] lexicon (próximo, máximo, fixo, exame) is documented residual.

Word-initial ⟨ex-⟩ before a vowel is [ez]: exame [eˈzami], exemplo [eˈzẽplu], existir [ezisˈt͡ʃiɾ], êxito [ˈezitu], exército [eˈzɛɾsitu] (Cunha & Cintra 1984, ch. 'Fonética': ⟨x⟩ 'soa como z' in the prefix ex- before a vowel; Mateus & d'Andrade 2000: ch.2, the voiced reading of ⟨x⟩ in exame/exemplo). The grapheme ⟨x⟩ carries five lexical readings and the beam takes the first, [ʃ], which is right after a diphthong (baixo, deixar) and word-initially (xadrez) but never in this prefix. Measured on the vox_communis pt-BR gold: 125 words start with ⟨ex⟩ plus a vowel letter and the gold writes [z] in all 125, [ʃ] in 0 (scripts/fold_pt_br_notation.py prints the count); 9 more start with ⟨hex⟩ and are also [z] in the gold. Gated to the ⟨x⟩ slot (grapheme), to a word-initial ⟨e/ê⟩ before it (preceded_by_grapheme plus preceded_by_2 = word_boundary) and to a vowel after it, so ⟨ex⟩ before a consonant (extra, exclusivo), a medial ⟨-ex-⟩ (sexo [ks], inexato) and the ⟨hex-⟩ words are untouched. The prefix inside a word (inexato, reexame) is also [z] but is not reachable by a neighbour condition without a morphological cut, and is left as documented residue.

notes: Brazilian Portuguese. Based directly on late Old Portuguese diaspora phonology. Key innovations: (1) Loss of coda R (ɾ→∅; later urban ɦ/ʁ in some dialects). (2) Coda sibilants remain alveolar (s, z), no universal palato-alveolar outcome. (3) L-vocalisation (l→w) strong and categorical in coda. (4) Palatalisation of /t, d/ > [t͡ʃ, d͡ʒ] before /i/. (5) Much weaker vowel reduction; loss of ɨ. (6) Final /e/→/i/ and /o/→/u/. (7) /rr/ is a posterior fricative, written [ʁ] (Barbosa & Albano 2004: 228 describe a velar fricative, voiced between voiced sounds). (8) Nasal vowel system preserved but with characteristic BR realisation. POST-LEXICAL ALLOPHONY (allophone_rules, base for the BR dialect specs via OVERLAY_BY_ID): final unstressed vowel raising — the near-close [ɪ]/[ʊ] selected word-finally by the positional map is realised as the standard BP close [i]/[u] (gato→[ˈɡatu], leite→[ˈlejt͡ʃi]). Targeting the reduced [ɪ]/[ʊ] (not underlying /e o/) leaves conservative dialects that retain a final [e]/[o] untouched, so the rule inherits cleanly. Deliberately kept in the positional map, NOT duplicated as allophone_rules to avoid double-application: /t d/ affrication before front vowels (grapheme-⟨i⟩ handled by the before_i positional rule) and coda /l/ vocalisation (l→w). The phoneme-conditioned refinement of affrication before a raised final ⟨e⟩ (dente→[ˈdẽt͡ʃi]) is left to the dialect-delta wave, where the non-palatalising nordeste varieties (recife/norte/ce) can opt out by rule id — expressing it in the base would silently re-impose affrication on those inheritors. Deliberately NOT modelled in the base: strong EP-style pretonic reduction (BP keeps distinct pretonic /e o/); coda /s/→[ʃ] chiado (a carioca/RJ dialect delta, not general BP — base stays alveolar [s]/[z]); coda /r/→[h~x] weak fricative (highly variable and, since the broad wikipron pt-BR gold transcribes coda /r/ as [ʁ], adding [h~x] regresses the only pt-BR gold — held as a dialect delta rather than shipped in the base). SIBILANTS ARE PLAIN ALVEOLAR. BP has one sibilant pair /s z/ (Barbosa & Albano 2004: 228, consonant chart, Alveolar column: saca [ˈsakɐ] / zaca [ˈzakɐ]). The apico-alveolar [s̺ z̺] belongs to the Galician-Portuguese four-sibilant system that roa-x-galaico-pt and pt-PT-x-medieval model, and to the northern EP dialects that retain it; it reached BP only by inheritance, because the base declared ⟨s c ç z⟩ but not the ⟨ss⟩ digraph and not positional ⟨c⟩ before ⟨e i⟩, so galaicopt ⟨ss⟩→[s̺] and medieval ⟨ce ci⟩→[s̺] fell through. Both are now declared here, matching the value all twelve pt-BR-x-* dialects already carry. ⟨ss⟩ and ⟨rr⟩ are DIGRAPHS, not geminates: Portuguese has no contrastive consonant length, ⟨ss⟩ spells /s/ where an intervocalic single ⟨s⟩ would be /z/ (isso [ˈisu]) and ⟨rr⟩ spells the strong rhotic (carro [ˈkaʁu] vs caro [ˈkaɾu], Barbosa & Albano 2004: 228), so there is no geminate for a collapse pass to remove and collapse_geminates stays unset. ⟨w⟩ occurs only in loans and names but is not silent — [w] in English loans, [v] in Germanic names — and without an entry the letter was deleted outright (web→[ˈeb], show→[ˈsu]).

sandhi_rules.name: final-s-voicing-before-voiced-consonant
sandhi_rules.notes: A word-final /S/ takes the voicing of a voiced consonant at the start of the next word: os dois [uz ˈdojs], as mesas [az ˈmezɐs]. Barbosa & Albano (2004: 229): 'The archiphoneme /S/ surfaces either as a voiced or as a voiceless alveolar fricative. As in most varieties, it tends to assimilate the voicing of the following sound.' Their transcribed passage writes 'duz doɪ̯z ɛɾɐ' for dos dois era, and keeps [s] before a voiceless consonant in 'maɪ̯s fɔɾtʃɪ' for mais forte (Barbosa & Albano 2004: 231). The voiced class is the class of BR_CODA_S_VOICED, which voices a coda /S/ inside a word. A regional spec that writes the strong rhotic voiceless ([x], [χ]) is outside the class, so the sibilant before it stays [s]. The rule matches the alveolar [s] only; a spec that writes the coda as [ʃ] keeps its output.

sandhi_rules.name: final-s-voicing-before-vowel
sandhi_rules.notes: A word-final /S/ before a word that starts with a vowel is [z]: dez anos [ˈdɛz ˈɐ̃nus], os amigos [uz aˈmiɡus]. Barbosa & Albano (2004: 229): 'it tends to assimilate the voicing of the following sound'. The transcribed passage writes 'doɪ̯z ɛɾɐ' for dois era and 'maɪ̯z u viaˈʒẽⁿt' for mais o viajante (Barbosa & Albano 2004: 231).

stress.notes: Acordo Ortográfico 1990 conventions: paroxytone default; written accents override; final -i/-u/-r/-l/-z/-x/-im/-om/-um/-ins/-ons/-uns and nasal diphthongs attract final stress. Unmarked -em/-ens/-am stay paroxytone (homem, homens, falam): an oxytone of more than one syllable in -em or -ens is written with an acute (Acordo Ortográfico 1990, Base VIII, 1.º c: deténs, haréns, provéns, também). DIPHTHONGS: declared so the bundled syllabifier counts nuclei correctly — without them every vowel run merges into one nucleus and co-e-lho is read as coe-lho, one syllable short, putting the stress and its vowel reduction on the wrong vowel. ⟨oe⟩ is hiatus, not a diphthong (Cunha & Cintra, §Ditongos). COMPOUNDS: a hyphenated compound is one prosodic word. Each element keeps its own stress and the last is the strongest (Bechara, Moderna Gramática Portuguesa, p. 340, quoted in Ciberdúvidas, resposta 28042), so compound_stress is "last": guarda-chuva gwˌaɾdɐˈʃuvɐ (Portal da Língua Portuguesa). IPA_DIPHTHONGS is empty: the grapheme table writes every diphthong with a glide ([aj], [uj], [ɐ̃w̃]), so two full vowels side by side in the transcription are always a hiatus, and the stress mark is placed with each IPA vowel as a nucleus of its own. Read with the orthographic list, the IPA [ui] of ⟨proíbe⟩ /pɾuibɨ/ and [iu] of ⟨viúva⟩ merge into one syllable and the mark lands a syllable early. The acute on a tonic ⟨i u⟩ after a vowel marks exactly this hiatus (Acordo Ortográfico 1990, Base X, 1.º: juízes, ruína, ciúme, miúdo, saída, baú). ONSETS: constrain_onsets is set, and onset_clusters names the complex onsets, so the bundled syllabifier divides a word as the silabificador plugin does and the transcription does not depend on whether the plugin is installed. A complex onset has two segments and the second is a non-nasal sonorant: 'No ataque podem se apresentar dois segmentos, dos quais o segundo é uma soante não nasal' (Curioletti & Sandri 2019, Cadernos do IL 59, PDF p. 6, citing Bisol 2013, not opened). Collischonn (2004: 66) says the same of a stop before a stop or a nasal (espectro, hipnose): 'a seqüência resultante não é admitida nem como ataque, nem como coda + ataque, pela estrutura canônica da sílaba em português'. So the first stop of ⟨pacto apto opção⟩ closes the syllable before it (pac.to, ap.to, op.ção), and BR_EPENTHESIS reads its stress there. ⟨st⟩ and ⟨dv⟩ have no sonorant second member, so escola is es.co.la and advogado is ad.vo.ga.do. CLOSED HIATUS: a tonic ⟨i u⟩ after a vowel takes no acute when it forms a syllable with the next consonant, and it is still a nucleus in hiatus: "As vogais tónicas/tônicas grafadas i e u das palavras oxítonas e paroxítonas não levam acento agudo quando, antecedidas de vogal com que não formam ditongo, constituem sílaba com a consoante seguinte, como é o caso de nh, l, m, n, r e z: bainha, moinho, rainha; adail, paul, Raul; Aboim, Coimbra, ruim; ainda, constituinte, oriundo, ruins, triunfo; atrair, demiurgo, influir, influirmos; juiz, raiz, etc." (Acordo Ortográfico 1990, Base X, 2.º, Portal da Língua Portuguesa, acordo.php?action=acordo&version=1990). closed_hiatus states it: the ⟨i u⟩ of ⟨ai au ei eu iu oi ui⟩ is split off before ⟨nh⟩, or before l m n r z when no vowel follows and the letter does not start ⟨lh rr⟩. ⟨ou⟩ is left out: Base X, 2.º gives no ⟨ou⟩ example, and the ⟨ou⟩ words of this shape are loans and foreign names (Lourdes, gourmet, tour). A following ⟨s⟩ is excluded (Base X, 1.º: "excetuando o caso de s"), so animais keeps its diphthong. The split holds only where the ⟨i u⟩ is stressed: Base XIV, 1.º says the spelling does not tell an atonic ⟨i u⟩ in hiatus from a diphthong (arruinar, faiscar), so an atonic one keeps the diphthong reading. FINAL DIPHTHONGS: a final ⟨iu ui⟩ after a vowel is one stressed diphthong, and the vowel before it is a nucleus of its own: "Prescinde-se do acento agudo nos ditongos tónicos/tônicos grafados iu e ui, quando precedidos de vogal: distraiu, instruiu, pauis (pl. de paul)." (Acordo Ortográfico 1990, Base X, 6.º, Portal da Língua Portuguesa, acordo.php?action=acordo&version=1990). So distraiu is dis-tra-iu and pauis is pa-uis, not dis-trai-u and pau-is. final_diphthongs states it for a word-final ⟨iu ui⟩, alone or before ⟨s⟩. A medial ⟨iu ui⟩ after a vowel is outside it: Base X, 4.º reads a tonic ⟨i u⟩ after a diphthong there (baiuca, cauila). A final one cannot have that reading unwritten, because Base X, 5.º writes the acute on a final tonic ⟨i u⟩ after a diphthong (Piauí, teiú, teiús). The split holds only where the diphthong is stressed. Barbosa & Albano (2004: 230): "A large list of oral diphthongs can be formed by combining the stressed oral vowels above with the offglides [ɪ̯] and [ʊ̯], *[iɪ̯] being the only impossible diphthong", so [iʊ̯] is a falling diphthong, and the transcribed passage gives desistiu [dʒizisˈtʃiʊ̯] with the stress on it (p. 231). TONIC AFTER DIPHTHONG: a stressed ⟨i u⟩ after a diphthong is a syllable of its own, and the diphthong keeps its glide: "Prescinde-se do acento agudo nas vogais tónicas/tônicas grafadas i e u das palavras paroxítonas, quando elas estão precedidas de ditongo: baiuca, boiuno, cauila (var. cauira), cheiinho (de cheio), saiinha (de saia)." (Acordo Ortográfico 1990, Base X, 4.º) and "Levam, porém, acento agudo as vogais tónicas/tônicas grafadas i e u quando, precedidas de ditongo, pertencem a palavras oxítonas e estão em posição final ou seguidas de s: Piauí, teiú, teiús, tuiuiú, tuiuiús. Obs.: Se, neste caso, a consoante final for diferente de s, tais vogais dispensam o acento agudo: cauim." (Base X, 5.º, Portal da Língua Portuguesa, acordo.php?action=acordo&version=1990). So baiuca is bai-u-ca and teiú is tei-ú. tonic_after_diphthong states it: where the stressed written syllable starts with ⟨i u í ú⟩ after a syllable that ends in a listed diphthong, the glide stays in the syllable before and the mark follows it. The rule reads only the place of the mark: the transcription already writes the glide and the vowel. An unstressed ⟨i u⟩ after a diphthong is outside it. NASAL DIPHTHONG ⟨ãi⟩: "Os ditongos representados por vogal com til e semivogal são quatro, considerando-se apenas a língua padrão contemporânea: ãe (usado em vocábulos oxítonos e derivados), ãi (usado em vocábulos anoxítonos e derivados), ão e õe. Exemplos: cães, Guimarães, mãe, mãezinha; cãibas, cãibeiro, cãibra, zãibo; [...]" (Acordo Ortográfico 1990, Base VII, 3 a), Portal da Língua Portuguesa, acordo.php?action=acordo&version=1990). So ⟨ãi⟩ is one nucleus, the diphthong of ⟨ãe⟩, and the grapheme table gives it the reading of ⟨ãe⟩. It is not in final_stress_endings, because Base VII, 3 a) uses it in anoxytones: cãibra is cãi-bra, stressed on the diphthong. Barbosa & Albano (2004: 230): "Nasalised diphthongs are formed by combining [ẽ ɐ̃ õ ũ] with the offglide [ɪ̯̃]", so [ɐ̃ɪ̯̃] is the nasal diphthong of both ⟨ãe⟩ and ⟨ãi⟩.
